newsitem.title: USA: Calif. agency cites Tosco over explosion.
newsitem.headline: Calif. agency cites Tosco over explosion.

text.p: The California Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA) said it cited Tosco Corp on Thursday for 22 safety violations over a fatal explosion at the company's Avon refinery in California.

Cal/OSHA imposed total penalties of $277,750 against Tosco Refining and Marketing Co. Cal/OSHA officials said they believed it was the highest penalty levied against an oil refinery company in California.
The January 21, 1997 explosion at the refinery's hydrocracker unit killed one Tosco employee and injured 46 Tosco and contractor workers, Cal/OSHA said.

"Our six-month inspection has shown us that Tosco failed to use recognized and generally accepted good engineering procedures in the operation of the company's hydrocracker unit," Cal/OSHA deputy chief Mark Carleson said.

Cal/OSHA cited Tosco for 22 alleged violations of state workplace safety regulations at the Avon refinery, near San Francisco. Three were classified as "willful serious" and carried the maximum penalties allowed of $70,000 each. Another sixteen of the violations were classified as serious under California's Code of Regulations and three were "general".
Under California law, Tosco may appeal Cal/OSHA citations and penalties within 15 working days to the Occupational Safety and Health Appeals Board in Sacramento.
A Tosco spokesman could not immediately be reached for comment.
Cal/OSHA said it had a concurrent criminal investigation of the incident under way through its Bureau of Investigation.

It said the findings from that investigation, which focused on possible criminal liability involved in the accident, would be handed over in a confidential report to the local district attorney's office for a determination as to whether criminal charges were appropriate.

The Cal/OSHA investigation found that the explosion and fire were caused when the temperature inside the hydrocracker unit passed 1,700 degrees Fahrenheit, exceeding the reactor's maximum safety level of 800 degrees Fahrenheit.
Temperature inside the reactor rose due to the process instability and was initially undetected by internal thermostats, Cal/OSHA said.

"While the investigation does not rule out the possibility of some aspect of operator error, it is clear that there remains a serious failure on the part of Tosco's management to implement the company's own internal safety policies," Cal/OSHA said in a statement.
The most serious violations identified by Cal/OSHA were that:
-- machinery and equipment in service were not kept in a safe operating condition
-- the company failed to have proper written procedures to address emergency operations, including emergency shutdowns
-- the company failed to respond or take action in a timely manner regarding written concerns expressed by employees about the hydrocracker unit

Cal/OSHA also said that inspection and testing procedures at the unit did not follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices and that employees assigned to the hydrocracker unit did not recieve required supplemental training at least every three years.
